title: Product manager situations
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Conflicting stakeholder requests
scenarios.prompt: Sales wants a feature for a large deal; Support wants the same engineering time to fix the top cause of tickets.

options.text: Decide yourself using impact estimates and explain the reasoning to both.
Bring both teams together to agree priorities in one meeting.
Split the capacity between both requests.
Escalate to your director for a call.

scenarios.title: Data versus intuition
scenarios.prompt: Usage data suggests a feature is rarely used. Your conversations with customers suggest the few who use it rely on it heavily.

options.text: Keep it; the qualitative signal matters more here.
Remove it; maintenance cost should follow usage.
Segment the data by customer value before deciding.
Hide it behind a setting and watch who complains.

scenarios.title: Launch date or quality
scenarios.prompt: A launch is set for next week. Engineering reports that the onboarding flow is functional but clunky.

options.text: Launch on time and schedule improvements for the following sprint.
Delay a week to polish onboarding; first impressions matter.
Launch to a small beta group first, then widen.
Launch on time with a guided walkthrough to cover the rough edges.

scenarios.title: Research contradicts the plan
scenarios.prompt: User research shows little interest in a feature your leadership has already announced internally.

options.text: Present the findings to leadership and recommend changing course.
Look for a smaller version of the feature that users did want.
Run a second study to make sure before raising it.
Build it as announced; the strategic reasons may outweigh research.

scenarios.title: Big customer request
scenarios.prompt: Your largest customer demands a custom feature no other customer has asked for, and hints they may leave without it.

options.text: Build it; keeping the account is worth the cost.
Decline politely and offer an integration or workaround.
Look for a general version that serves other customers too.
Ask the account team for the real revenue risk before deciding.

scenarios.title: Prioritisation method
scenarios.prompt: The team asks how you decide roadmap order. Today it is mostly your judgement.

options.text: Introduce a scoring framework and publish the scores.
Explain your reasoning more often, but keep judgement-based decisions.
Run a quarterly prioritisation workshop with the team.
Keep it as it is; frameworks give false precision.

scenarios.title: Engineering pushes back on a spec
scenarios.prompt: Engineers say your spec is too detailed and leaves them no room to find a better solution.

options.text: Rewrite it as a problem statement with goals and constraints only.
Keep the detail; it reflects decisions already validated with users.
Mark which parts are fixed and which are open for engineering to shape.
Hold a working session to co-design the solution.

scenarios.title: Metric drops after launch
scenarios.prompt: A week after a launch, conversion has dropped two percent. The cause is unclear.

options.text: Roll back immediately and investigate afterwards.
Investigate for two more days before acting; it may be noise.
Roll back for half of traffic to test the cause.
Keep it; the launch has other long-term benefits.

scenarios.title: Executive's pet idea
scenarios.prompt: An executive pitches a feature idea in a hallway conversation and asks when it can ship.

options.text: Tell them honestly it does not fit the current strategy and why.
Say you will evaluate it alongside other ideas and report back.
Add it to the roadmap; executive support helps the team.
Ask what problem they want to solve and explore that instead.

scenarios.title: Discovery or delivery
scenarios.prompt: Delivery pressure leaves you no time for customer discovery. You worry the roadmap is drifting from real needs.

options.text: Protect a fixed weekly slot for customer calls, no matter what.
Ask a designer or researcher to run discovery for you.
Do discovery opportunistically when delivery quietens down.
Use support tickets and sales notes as a lightweight substitute.

scenarios.title: Competitor launch
scenarios.prompt: A competitor launches a feature your customers have occasionally asked about. The sales team is anxious.

options.text: Fast-track a comparable feature this quarter.
Interview customers about it before changing the roadmap.
Give sales talking points and keep the roadmap unchanged.
Look for a differentiated answer rather than a copy.

scenarios.title: Inconclusive experiment
scenarios.prompt: An A/B test ends with no significant difference. The new variant is cleaner but costlier to maintain.

options.text: Ship the new variant; cleaner experiences pay off over time.
Keep the old variant; no proven gain means no change.
Extend the test to get more statistical power.
Ask the team which variant they would rather maintain.
